findings.title: Write-only instance attribute `self._contract_categorical_levels` is never read anywhere
findings.description: `self._contract_categorical_levels` is initialised in `__init__` (line 369) and reassigned in `run()` (line 426: `self._contract_categorical_levels = dict(prepared.categorical_levels)`), but it is never read in production code or tests. A repo-wide search for the name returns only those two write sites. Its two sibling snapshot attributes set on the adjacent lines are genuinely consumed (`_contract_feature_dtypes` at line 1473 in `_feature_dtypes_for_contract`, `_contract_target_dtype` at line 1477 in `_target_dtype_for_contract`), but the categorical-levels snapshot has no reader: the categorical domains that actually reach the artifact/signature writers flow through a different path entirely — `prepared.categorical_levels` is passed straight into `_save_artifacts` (line 509), and `_log_to_mlflow`/`_save_artifacts` recompute via `_categorical_levels_for_contract`. The docstring at lines 365-370 justifies the snapshot trio generically, but the categorical-levels member is swept along unused. The `dict(...)` copy at line 426 is therefore wasted work and the attribute is misleading state.
findings.evidence: Grep for `_contract_categorical_levels` across the whole repo (src + tests) yields exactly two hits, both assignments (line 369 init, line 426 in run); zero reads. Contrast `_contract_feature_dtypes` (read at line 1473) and `_contract_target_dtype` (read at line 1477). The live categorical-levels value used downstream comes from `prepared.categorical_levels` (run() line 509 -> _save_artifacts) and `_categorical_levels_for_contract`, never from `self._contract_categorical_levels`.
findings.est_reduction: ~2 lines (remove the line 369 declaration and the line 426 assignment)
findings.behavior_preservation: No behavioural change: the attribute has no readers, so deleting both writes cannot affect any artifact, signature, contract, or test output. Pure dead-state removal.

findings.title: Split parquet leaks if the bare `os.unlink(data_path)` at line 821 raises after the split file was written
findings.description: `_split_data` writes the split parquet to `split_path` (lines 789-807) and then, on success, removes the prepared input with a bare `os.unlink(data_path)` (line 821) — bypassing the loud-but-safe `_remove_temp_parquet` helper used everywhere else in this module. If that `os.unlink` raises an `OSError` (e.g. a transient Windows file lock, EBUSY, or a permission/network-FS hiccup on the temp dir), the exception propagates out of `_split_data` BEFORE it can `return _SplitResult(...)`. Because `_SplitResult` was never returned, `run()`'s `split_result` stays `None`, so the `finally` -> `_cleanup_owned_temp_parquets(prepared, split_result)` only considers `prepared` and never sees `split_path`. The freshly written split parquet (potentially multi-GB) is therefore orphaned in the OS temp dir — exactly the failure mode the remediation-4b.6 cleanup net (run() lines 550-558) was built to prevent. The same bare-unlink pattern at `_prepare_data` line 707 has the analogous shape, though there `data_path` is still tracked by `prepared` so the leak is narrower. The dedicated cleanup test suite (tests/test_training_temp_cleanup.py) exercises cancellation and metrics/validation failures but has no case where the inline `os.unlink` itself fails, so this window is untested.
findings.evidence: _split_data: split_path created (789-794) and written via bounded_sink (803); on the failure branch only split_path is removed (812-814); on success line 821 does `os.unlink(data_path)` then line 824 `return _SplitResult(... owns_tmp=True)`. If line 821 throws, the function raises pre-return, so run() (474-478) gets no split_result; the finally at 558 calls _cleanup_owned_temp_parquets(prepared, None) which builds candidates only from prepared (573-576) — split_path is never a candidate and leaks. Every other temp deletion in the module routes through _remove_temp_parquet (which swallows OSError to a warning), but lines 707 and 821 use a raw os.unlink.

findings.title: `asdict(self.split_config) if self.split_config else {}` — the `else {}` branch is unreachable and contradicts the unconditional `self.split_config.<attr>` access 17 lines below in the same call
findings.description: In `_log_to_mlflow`, the `metadata = ModelCardMetadata(...)` construction guards the split_config field with `split_config=asdict(self.split_config) if self.split_config else {}`. `self.split_config` is assigned unconditionally in `__init__` (lines 358-363): it is always a `SplitConfig` — a passed `SplitConfig`, a `SplitConfig(**split)` built from a dict, or `SplitConfig()` — and is never `None`. `SplitConfig` is a plain `@dataclass` (src/haute/modelling/_split.py:12-13) with no `__bool__` or `__len__`, so any instance is always truthy. The `else {}` branch is therefore dead. Worse, it is internally inconsistent: the very same `log_experiment(...)` call dereferences `self.split_config` WITHOUT any guard at lines 1568-1570 (`self.split_config.strategy`, `self.split_config.validation_size`, `self.split_config.holdout_size`). If `self.split_config` could ever be falsy/None (the premise of the line-1551 guard), those three accesses would raise `AttributeError` first — proving the guard is both unnecessary and contradictory. The simplification is to drop the guard: `split_config=asdict(self.split_config)`.
findings.evidence: __init__ lines 358-363: `if isinstance(split, SplitConfig): self.split_config = split / elif isinstance(split, dict): self.split_config = SplitConfig(**split) / else: self.split_config = SplitConfig()` — every branch sets a SplitConfig, none sets None. _split.py:12-13 shows `@dataclass\nclass SplitConfig:` with no __bool__/__len__ override (grep found none) ⇒ always truthy. Same method, line 1551 guards it, while lines 1568-1570 inside the immediately-following `log_experiment(...)` call read `self.split_config.strategy / .validation_size / .holdout_size` unconditionally. The guarded and unguarded usages cannot both be correct; the unguarded ones are correct, so the guard is dead.
findings.est_reduction: -0 to -1 LOC (replace `asdict(self.split_config) if self.split_config else {}` with `asdict(self.split_config)`); removes one dead branch and the false implication that split_config can be None.
findings.behavior_preservation: Behaviour-identical for all reachable states: self.split_config is always a truthy SplitConfig, so the expression already always evaluates to `asdict(self.split_config)`. No call path can make the `else {}` fire (run() is the only caller of _log_to_mlflow and it uses the same self instance whose __init__ guaranteed a SplitConfig).

findings.title: `model_path=result.model_path or None` — `result.model_path` is always a non-empty string on the only call path, so the `or None` fallback never fires
findings.description: In `_log_to_mlflow`, `log_experiment(...)` is called with `model_path=result.model_path or None`. `_log_to_mlflow` is invoked only from `run()` (line 545), and the `TrainResult` it receives is built at lines 512-540 with `model_path=str(model_path)`, where `model_path` is the `Path` returned by `_save_artifacts` (always `output_dir / f"{self.name}{ext}"`, a non-empty path). `str(Path(...))` is therefore always a non-empty string, which is truthy, so `result.model_path or None` always evaluates to `result.model_path`. The `or None` fallback is dead. (`TrainResult.model_path` is even typed `str`, not `str | None`, at line 174, reinforcing that None is not an expected value.) This is lower-confidence than the split_config finding because `TrainResult` is a public dataclass that an external caller could in principle construct with `model_path=""` before calling `_log_to_mlflow` directly; on the actual in-tree call path the branch is unreachable.
findings.evidence: run() line 505-510 binds `model_path = self._save_artifacts(...)` (a Path); _save_artifacts returns `output_dir / f"{self.name}{ext}"` (line 1324/1360). TrainResult constructed at 512 with `model_path=str(model_path)` ⇒ non-empty str. TrainResult.model_path annotated `str` (line 174). _log_to_mlflow is reached only via run() line 545 with that same result, so `result.model_path` is always a truthy non-empty string and `... or None` never yields None.
findings.est_reduction: -0 LOC (replace `result.model_path or None` with `result.model_path`); removes a dead fallback.
findings.behavior_preservation: Behaviour-identical on the in-tree call path (result.model_path is always a non-empty string). Only a direct external caller passing model_path="" would observe a difference, which the production pipeline never does.

findings.title: _ave_categorical_bins sentinel '__MISSING__' collides with a real category of that name
findings.description: In _ave_categorical_bins the null-handling uses a string sentinel: `col.cast(pl.Utf8).fill_null("__MISSING__")` (line 567), and a group whose category equals `"__MISSING__"` is later relabeled to "Missing" (line 590). If the categorical feature contains a genuine category whose string value is literally `"__MISSING__"`, those real rows are merged into the same group as the true nulls and then presented under the label "Missing". This silently conflates two distinct populations (real value vs. missing) in the Actual-vs-Expected diagnostic, producing a misleading AvE row. The collision is a stringly-typed sentinel rather than an out-of-band null marker, so it is data-dependent and not guarded against. Note _ave_numeric_bins is NOT affected (its "Missing" label is for NaN-masked numeric rows, which cannot collide with a numeric value).
findings.evidence: Line 567: `"cat": col.cast(pl.Utf8).fill_null("__MISSING__")`. Group-by at lines 573-581 keys on this column, so a row with the real string `"__MISSING__"` shares the null group's key. Line 590: `label = "Missing" if row["cat"] == "__MISSING__" else row["cat"]` — both the genuine-null group and any real `"__MISSING__"` category render as "Missing". The two populations are summed together in `exposure`/`sum_actual`/`sum_predicted` and cannot be distinguished downstream.

coverage.notes: Exhaustively reviewed all 23 in-scope functions. Verified deviance formulas (_poisson_deviance, _tweedie_deviance Poisson/Gamma/general-p/p>2 branches) numerically equal to sklearn including y_true==0 cases. Confirmed tie-corrected Gini/Lorenz aggregation (_aggregated_lorenz_points) is permutation-invariant and float-negation-safe (inputs are _as_float_array'd before -sort_key). Verified compute_residuals_histogram's separate digitize-based weighted bins agree exactly with np.histogram counts including the inclusive right edge, and bincount(minlength=n_bins) cannot overflow the counts list. Confirmed compute_ave_per_feature keeps df and y_true/y_pred/weight aligned after the shared finite-mask filter (caller passes a df whose height matches y_true). Confirmed RandomState(42) is locally instantiated in compute_actual_vs_predicted and compute_pdp (no shared global RNG state) and Lorenz downsampling always retains first/last points. Degenerate cases (empty, single-row, zero total weight/loss, constant predictor/target) all return documented degenerate values; fully-non-finite input fails loud per policy. Negative-target Gini is finite (domain-out-of-scope, not a defect). Only genuine defect found is the low-severity '__MISSING__' sentinel collision in _ave_categorical_bins; the np.nanmin/nanmax in _ave_numeric_bins are harmlessly redundant (NaN never enters a numeric bin) and not reported.

findings.title: render_horizontal_bars_svg scales the axis by abs(value) but orders/selects bars by raw signed value, so a single large-magnitude negative inflates the scale while being sorted last or dropped
findings.description: The function sorts items by RAW value descending and truncates to max_items: `items = sorted(data, key=lambda d: d.get(value_key, 0), reverse=True)[:max_items]` (line 446). The axis scale is then computed from the ABSOLUTE value: `max_val = max(abs(d[value_key]) for d in items)` (line 455), and each bar width is `plot_w * abs(item[value_key]) / max_val` (lines 473-474), while the printed value label uses the SIGNED value `{item[value_key]:.4f}` (line 489). These two sort/scale conventions disagree for mixed-sign data: a feature with a large negative value (e.g. -50) is the LEAST important by raw-descending sort (placed at the bottom, or dropped entirely when there are more than max_items rows), yet it sets max_val=50, shrinking every positive bar toward zero and making them visually near-invisible. The chart thus draws bar magnitudes (abs) and bar ordering (signed) that tell contradictory stories about 'importance'. Reachable via diag.feature_importance_loss (CatBoost LossFunctionChange), which the caller _model_card.py:201-205 routes through this function and which can legitimately be negative when a feature's removal would reduce loss (importance/mean_abs_shap are always >=0, so those two callers are unaffected).
findings.evidence: Confirmed with synthetic data: render_horizontal_bars_svg([{feature:'strong_negative',v:-100},{feature:'tiny_pos_1',v:0.3},{feature:'tiny_pos_2',v:0.2}], max_items=2) renders only ['tiny_pos_1','tiny_pos_2'] — 'strong_negative' (|v|=100, the largest magnitude) is dropped because raw-descending sort places it last, yet had it been kept it would set max_val=100 and crush the others. With max_items not limiting, top->bottom order for v=[0.5,-0.9,0.1] is ['A','C','B'] even though B has the biggest |v|. Upstream producer (_algorithms.py:639-644 feature_importance_typed) also sorts by raw value desc, so the chart's ordering is consistent with the system, but the abs-based scale at line 455 is the lone inconsistency. tests/test_charts.py::test_negative_values only asserts well-formed XML, not scale/ordering, so this is uncovered.

findings.title: _render_dual_axis_chart computes a truncated `display` label for every x tick but the non-rotated branch ignores it and emits the full untruncated label, so long non-rotated x-labels render at full length (overlap/overflow) while `display` is dead on that path
findings.description: At line 210 the loop unconditionally computes `display = _truncate_label(str(label), 15)`. The rotated branch (lines 213-218) renders `_escape(display)` (truncated), but the non-rotated branch (lines 220-224) renders `_escape(str(label))` — the FULL, untruncated label. Consequently the `display` computation is wasted work on the common non-rotated path (a small per-tick allocation), and, more importantly, the two branches apply inconsistent truncation policy: rotated labels are capped at 15 chars while non-rotated labels are emitted verbatim. A caller that passes long labels with rotate_labels=False (e.g. render_double_lift_svg, which is hard-wired to the non-rotated path) renders the full string centered under each point, so long labels overlap their neighbours and overflow the plot width, whereas the same labels under rotation would have been truncated. This is distinct from the known AvE-label-truncation finding (which concerns rotated labels with a shared 15-char prefix colliding AFTER truncation); here the defect is the non-rotated branch never truncating at all and `display` being unused on that branch.
findings.evidence: Confirmed: render_double_lift_svg([{decile:'VERY_LONG_DECILE_LABEL_0123456789',...},{decile:'B',...}]) (always non-rotated) emits the full 'VERY_LONG_DECILE_LABEL_0123456789' in the SVG and never the truncated form 'VERY_LONG_DECIL…'. The same chart with rotate_labels=True emits the truncated '…' form and not the full label. So `display` at line 210 is computed-but-unused whenever rotate_labels is False, and non-rotated long labels are not length-bounded.
findings.behavior_preservation: Either hoist the `display` computation into the rotated branch only (eliminating dead work on the non-rotated path) or use `_escape(display)` in BOTH branches so non-rotated long labels are truncated consistently (a behaviour change that bounds label width). The truncation width (15) and rotation decision are otherwise unchanged.
findings.est_reduction: ~1 line of dead computation removed from the hot non-rotated path; resolves the truncate-policy asymmetry between the two branches

findings.title: early_stopping_rounds default block collapses to a single assignment (pop + guard are no-ops)
findings.description: Inside CatBoostAlgorithm.fit, the block `if eval_pool is not None and "early_stopping_rounds" not in model_params:` is only entered when the key is ABSENT from model_params. It then does `early_stop = model_params.pop("early_stopping_rounds", 50)` — but since the key is guaranteed absent (that is the branch condition), `.pop` unconditionally returns the default 50; it never pops anything. The subsequent guard `if early_stop and early_stop > 0:` is therefore `if 50 and 50 > 0`, which is always True. The whole 3-line body is exactly equivalent to `model_params["early_stopping_rounds"] = 50`. The pop, the local, and the conditional are dead complexity that imply a configurability (e.g. honouring/clearing a user-supplied value) that the outer guard has already excluded.
findings.evidence: Line 513 guard: `"early_stopping_rounds" not in model_params` -> key absent. Line 514: `model_params.pop("early_stopping_rounds", 50)` on an absent key returns 50 (default) and removes nothing. Line 515: `if early_stop and early_stop > 0` with early_stop==50 is always True. Line 516 then sets it to 50. Test tests/test_algorithms_coverage.py:475 `test_early_stopping_rounds_default` asserts only the net effect `captured_params.get("early_stopping_rounds") == 50`, so collapsing to one assignment preserves behaviour.
findings.est_reduction: 3 lines -> 1 line (drop the pop, the local, and the always-true conditional).
findings.behavior_preservation: Net effect is identical: when an eval pool is present and the user did not set early_stopping_rounds, the param becomes 50. The replaced internals are provably unreachable/constant (key absent by the guard; 50 is truthy/positive), so no input changes the outcome. The existing default test continues to pass.

findings.title: feature_importance and feature_importance_typed are byte-identical except the get_feature_importance call
findings.description: CatBoostAlgorithm.feature_importance (617-625) and feature_importance_typed (627-644) share the same body: read `model.feature_names_`, `zip(names, importances)`, `sorted(..., key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)`, then `[{"feature": name, "importance": float(imp)} for name, imp in pairs]`. The only difference is the importances source: `model.get_feature_importance()` vs `model.get_feature_importance(data=pool, type=type_name)`. The sort+projection tail can be factored into one private helper (e.g. `_rank_importances(names, importances)`) called by both, removing the duplicated ranking/formatting logic.
findings.evidence: Lines 618-625 and 637-644 differ only at line 619 (`model.get_feature_importance()`) vs line 638 (`model.get_feature_importance(data=pool, type=type_name)`); the `names = model.feature_names_`, the `sorted(zip(...), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)` and the return comprehension are textually identical.
findings.est_reduction: ~8 duplicated lines reduced to a shared 3-line helper (net ~5 lines).
findings.behavior_preservation: Both methods keep their exact public signatures and call the same CatBoost API with the same arguments; only the shared post-processing (sort by importance desc, project to {feature, importance:float}) is centralised, producing byte-identical output lists.

findings.title: GPU loss-history 'iteration' is 0-based int while CPU callback writes 1-based float, mis-aligning the loss-curve x-axis between paths
findings.description: The CPU progress callback (_CatBoostProgressCallback.after_iteration) records `history_entry = {"iteration": float(it)}` with `it = info.iteration + 1` — i.e. 1-based and float. The GPU reconstruction branch in CatBoostAlgorithm.fit (lines 567-581) instead appends `{"iteration": i}` where `i` is the 0-based enumerate index and an int. The two paths therefore emit different `iteration` conventions for the same logical training. render_loss_curve_svg (src/haute/modelling/_charts.py:310/369/378) uses this `iteration` field directly as the x-coordinate (`x_pos(iterations[i])`), and the best-iteration marker is positioned with `x_pos(best_iteration)` (line 386-387) where best_iteration comes from CatBoost's 0-based `best_iteration_`. Consequently the marker is consistent with the curve on GPU (both 0-based) but off-by-one on CPU (curve 1-based, marker 0-based), and the same model trained on CPU vs GPU renders its x-axis shifted by one. The divergence is a contract mismatch between two in-scope code paths writing the same loss_history schema.
findings.evidence: Line 190-194: `it = info.iteration + 1` then `history_entry = {"iteration": float(it)}` (1-based, float). Lines 573-575/579-581: `if i >= len(loss_history): loss_history.append({"iteration": i})` with `for i, v in enumerate(values)` (0-based, int). _charts.py:386 `clamped = min(best_iteration, x_max); bx = x_pos(clamped)` plots best_iteration on the same axis as `iterations` (line 310 `d.get("iteration", i)`), so a 1-based curve + 0-based marker (CPU) is misaligned by one.

findings.location: src/haute/modelling/_mlflow_log.py:376-381 (register_model call in log_experiment); contrast _log_model_with_signature at 457-462 (catboost.log_model artifact_path="model") and 471-476 (pyfunc.log_model artifact_path="model" + log_artifact at run root)
findings.title: Databricks model registration uses the source filename basename, not the artifact_path the model was actually logged under — registration fails for CatBoost models
findings.description: log_experiment registers the model with source URI f"runs:/{run.info.run_id}/{Path(model_path).name}" (e.g. runs:/<id>/model.cbm). But the model is logged by _log_model_with_signature via mlflow.catboost.log_model(cb_model=..., artifact_path="model", ...), which writes an MLflow model *directory* at artifact path 'model' (containing MLmodel + the serialized CatBoost file) and never logs a top-level 'model.cbm' artifact (the CatBoost branch returns at line 462 without any log_artifact). The correct registration source for that logged model is runs:/<id>/model, not runs:/<id>/model.cbm. On Databricks (the only branch where register_model runs: line 376 gates on backend=="databricks"), mlflow.register_model("runs:/<id>/model.cbm", ...) resolves a non-existent artifact path and fails. The non-CatBoost branch (.rsglm/pyfunc) does log the raw file at the run root via mlflow.log_artifact(str(model_file)) (line 476), so runs:/<id>/<name>.rsglm exists as a bare artifact — but that is the raw model file, not the logged pyfunc model at runs:/<id>/model, so registering it as a UC model is still the wrong source. Both flavors should register runs:/<id>/model.
findings.evidence: Line 379: f"runs:/{run.info.run_id}/{Path(model_path).name}" -> for model_path ending in 'model.cbm' this is runs:/<id>/model.cbm. Lines 457-462 (CatBoost branch): mlflow.catboost.log_model(cb_model=cat_model, artifact_path="model", signature=signature); return — no log_artifact, so the only model artifact is the directory 'model/' (flavor format), and there is NO 'model.cbm' file artifact at the run root. Therefore the registration source path 'model.cbm' does not exist among the run's artifacts and register_model raises. tests/test_mlflow_log.py:514-517 enshrines the wrong URI by asserting register_model is called with "runs:/abc123/model.cbm" while mlflow.catboost.log_model is mocked away, so the mismatch is never exercised end-to-end. The fix is to register f"runs:/{run.info.run_id}/model" (the artifact_path both log_model calls use).
findings.behavior_preservation: n/a (correctness fix changes the registration URI to runs:/<id>/model; the existing test assertion at tests/test_mlflow_log.py:514-517 would need updating to the correct path).

findings.title: Temp JSON file leaks when json.dump raises — cleanup try/finally wraps only log_artifact, not the dump that created the file
findings.description: _log_json_artifact opens tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(..., delete=False) and calls json.dump(data, f, indent=2) inside the with-block. The os.unlink(f.name) cleanup lives in a separate try/finally that begins AFTER the with-block and only guards the mlflow.log_artifact call. If json.dump raises inside the with-block (data is typed Any; a non-JSON-serializable value such as a numpy np.int64 / np.float32 / np.ndarray embedded in a diagnostic dict raises TypeError), the file has already been created on disk and is closed by the with-exit, but the unlink is never reached — the temp file is orphaned in the OS temp directory. The created file is also not removed on the exception path the way log_artifact failures are. In normal operation the diagnostic producers cast to native float() (e.g. _algorithms.py feature_importance/shap_summary), so this is primarily a defense-in-depth/cleanup-contract gap rather than a guaranteed production leak, but the helper's own try/finally clearly intends to always clean up and fails to do so for the write step.
findings.evidence: Lines 140-150: `with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(mode="w", suffix=".json", prefix=f"{prefix}_", delete=False) as f: json.dump(data, f, indent=2)` then `try: mlflow.log_artifact(f.name, artifact_dir) finally: os.unlink(f.name)`. Because delete=False, the file persists after the with-block; the only unlink is in the finally attached to log_artifact. A TypeError from json.dump (json.dump(np.int64(5), f) raises 'Object of type int64 is not JSON serializable') propagates out before reaching the try/finally, leaking f.name. A correct shape wraps the NamedTemporaryFile usage (write + log) in a single try whose finally unlinks, or writes to a directory cleaned via try/finally around the whole body.
findings.behavior_preservation: n/a (correctness/cleanup fix; on the success path behavior is unchanged).

findings.title: Unreachable `list(invalid_series or [])` fallback in validate_categorical_value_domains is dead and would itself raise if reached
findings.description: After `examples = streaming_collect(lazy.select(invalid_example_exprs), ...)`, the loop does `invalid_series = examples[column][0]`. Every expr in `invalid_example_exprs` ends in `.implode()`, so each output column has dtype List(String); indexing `[0]` into a List-typed Series ALWAYS returns an inner `polars.Series`, which always exposes `.to_list()`. Therefore `hasattr(invalid_series, 'to_list')` is invariably True and the `else list(invalid_series or [])` branch is never taken. Worse, the fallback is not even a valid safety net: if it ever did run on a non-empty Series, `invalid_series or []` raises `TypeError: the truth value of a Series is ambiguous` (verified: bool() on a polars Series of any length raises). `implode()` also never yields a null/None element (an all-valid or empty frame produces an empty inner Series, not None — verified), so the `or []` None-guard is doubly dead. This is exactly the kind of incorrect, hard-to-notice fallback CLAUDE.md forbids; the branch should be removed and replaced with a direct `invalid_series.to_list()`.
findings.evidence: Empirically: for an empty input frame, `lazy.select(value_expr.filter(invalid).unique().head(10).implode())` yields shape (1,1) with `examples[column][0]` == an empty `pl.Series` (has `.to_list()` -> []); for invalid rows it's a non-empty `pl.Series`. `bool(pl.Series(['east']) or [])` -> TypeError 'truth value of a Series is ambiguous'. Thus the else-branch is unreachable, and unsound if reached.
findings.behavior_preservation: Behaviour identical for every reachable input (the else branch can never execute on the polars data path); removing it only deletes an unreachable, unsound fallback.

findings.title: `truncated` flag is a false positive when exactly max_examples distinct invalid values exist
findings.description: The error context computes `truncated=len(invalid_values) >= max_examples`. But `invalid_values` is produced by `.head(max_examples)`, so `len(invalid_values)` can never exceed `max_examples`; the comparison is true precisely when `len == max_examples`. That condition is reached both when the invalid set was genuinely larger than `max_examples` (truly truncated) AND when there were exactly `max_examples` distinct invalid values with none dropped. In the latter case `truncated=True` is wrong and would mislead an operator/log consumer into believing more invalid levels exist than were reported. The standard fix is to materialise `max_examples + 1` examples and report `truncated = len(examples) > max_examples` (then trim for display).
findings.evidence: Line 456-461 builds `... .head(max_examples) .implode()`. Line 469-473 yields at most `max_examples` items. Line 481 sets `truncated=len(invalid_values) >= max_examples`, so a column with exactly `max_examples` distinct out-of-domain values reports `truncated=True` despite the list being complete.

findings.title: max_examples <= 0 silently disables the categorical-domain check (no-op validator)
findings.description: `validate_categorical_value_domains` caps examples with `.head(max_examples)`. If a caller passes `max_examples=0`, `.head(0)` returns an empty Series for every column, so `invalid_values` is always `[]`, `if invalid_values:` is never true, and the function returns without raising even when the frame contains values outside the declared domain — a safety check silently becomes a no-op. A negative `max_examples` is worse: polars `.head(-k)` drops the LAST k rows (verified: `Series.head(-1)` returns all-but-last), so the validator under-reports invalid values and the `truncated` flag becomes meaningless. No current in-tree caller passes a non-default value (`_validate_runtime_categorical_values` and `_assert_runtime_contract_matches` omit it), so this is latent rather than active, but given the module's fail-loud mandate the function should reject `max_examples <= 0` instead of degrading into a silent pass.
findings.evidence: Param default is `max_examples: int = 10`. `Series('x',['a','b','c','d']).head(0).to_list()` == [] and `.head(-1).to_list()` == ['a','b','c'] (verified). With max_examples=0 the per-column `.head(0)` yields empty implode -> invalid_values==[] -> no raise even for out-of-domain data.

findings.title: `ordered` list in normalise_categorical_levels is redundant with `seen`
findings.description: Inside the per-column loop, both a `seen` set and an `ordered` list are maintained. Duplicate detection uses `seen` (line 363); the emptiness guard uses `if not ordered` (line 373); the final output is `sorted(level for level in ordered if level is not None)` plus an appended `None` (lines 380-384). Because the output is fully re-sorted, `ordered`'s insertion order is never used — every consumer of `ordered` could read `seen` instead (`if not seen` is equivalent since seen and ordered always have identical membership and are empty together). `ordered` (and its `.append` on every iteration) is therefore pure overhead and can be deleted, deriving the result solely from `seen`.
findings.evidence: Lines 352/372 build `ordered`; line 373 `if not ordered`; line 381 `sorted(level for level in ordered if level is not None)`. `seen` (lines 353/363/371/383) already holds the exact same elements, and the final list is produced by `sorted(...)`, discarding any order `ordered` preserved.
findings.est_reduction: ~3 lines (drop the `ordered` list and its append; use `seen` for the emptiness check and the sorted comprehension)
findings.behavior_preservation: Identical output: duplicates already rejected before insertion so seen==set(ordered); sorted() makes insertion order irrelevant; `not seen` <=> `not ordered`.

findings.title: include_main all-or-nothing guard still causes duplicate-main-effect singularity on partial factor overlap
findings.description: The guard sets include_main=False only when ALL interaction factors are already in the main `terms` dict, and otherwise forwards include_main (default True). But RustyStats' include_main=True adds main effects for EVERY factor in the interaction. When an interaction mixes factors that ARE already standalone main terms with factors that are NOT (a partial overlap), include_main=True re-adds the main effect for the already-present factor, producing exactly the duplicated main effect / perfect-collinearity / singular-matrix error the docstring (lines 69-74, 89-90) claims to prevent. The guard's premise ('set include_main=True when at least one factor is NOT in terms') is incomplete: a single missing factor flips the whole interaction to include_main=True even though the other, present, factors must NOT get their main effects re-added. RustyStats exposes include_main only as one boolean for the whole interaction, so the present design cannot add only the missing main effects — the partial-overlap case is structurally mishandled.
findings.evidence: terms={'age': {...}} (age is a standalone main term); config=[{'factors':['age','region'],'include_main':True}] with 'region' not in terms. Loop (82-87) builds rs_int={'age':{...copy...},'region':{'type':'categorical'}}. all_in_terms = all(f in terms for f in ['age','region']) = False (region missing). else-branch (95): rs_int['include_main']=interaction.get('include_main',True)=True. RustyStats then ADDS main effects for both age and region; age already exists as a standalone term => duplicate main effect for age => singular matrix at fit. This exact config is constructed in tests/test_rustystats_algorithm.py:92-98 (test_include_main_when_factor_not_in_terms), which asserts only result[0]['include_main'] is True and never attempts a fit, so the singularity is unexercised.

findings.title: Primary coefficients_table path emits partial rows (missing required stat keys) when coef_table() column names are not in key_map, contradicting the strict fallback contract
findings.description: GLMInferenceUnavailableError's docstring and the fallback path (lines 351-390) enforce that every emitted coefficient row carries ALL six normalized fields (feature, coefficient, std_error, z_value, p_value, significance) — the frontend's GlmCoefficientRow declares all six as REQUIRED (frontend/src/api/types.ts:317-324). But the PRIMARY path does no such validation: it maps each raw column with `key_map.get(k, k.lower().replace(' ','_'))` and returns whatever results. If RustyStats names any column outside the hard-coded key_map (e.g. the significance column as 'Signif.' with a trailing dot, a blank ' ' header as R uses for stars, or a renamed z column), that field is emitted under a non-canonical snake_cased key and the canonical key is silently absent. The two emission paths thus enforce opposite contracts: the fallback raises rather than ship a partial row, while the primary path ships partial rows. Because _training_job.py:1237-1241 records coefficients_table() output verbatim into glm_coefficients and the row is shipped to the UI, a future/changed RustyStats column header degrades to a malformed payload instead of the loud GLMInferenceUnavailableError the design intends.
findings.evidence: Lines 331-338: `coef_df = model.coef_table(); raw = coef_df.to_dicts(); return [{key_map.get(k, k.lower().replace(' ','_')): v for k,v in row.items()} for row in raw]`. key_map (319-329) hard-codes exact strings ('Signif' -> 'significance', 'Pr(>|z|)' -> 'p_value', 'z'/'z value'/'z.value' -> 'z_value'). Any unlisted header H yields key H.lower().replace(' ','_') (e.g. 'Signif.' -> 'signif.'), so 'significance' never appears. No post-normalization check verifies the six required keys exist on each row before returning. Contrast: the fallback (367-375) explicitly raises GLMInferenceUnavailableError rather than ship rows missing a stat. Frontend GlmCoefficientRow (types.ts:317-324) lists all six as non-optional.

findings.title: set(cat_features) rebuilt once per feature inside the list-comprehension filter
findings.description: `continuous = [f for f in features if f not in set(cat_features)]` places set(cat_features) in the comprehension's filter predicate, which CPython re-evaluates for every element of `features` — rebuilding the set O(len(features)) times instead of once. Hoisting the set out of the comprehension (compute `cat_set = set(cat_features)` once, then `[f for f in features if f not in cat_set]`) preserves behaviour exactly and makes the membership test O(1) against a single set. The codebase already uses this hoisted idiom elsewhere (e.g. _auto_terms line 48 `cat_set = set(cat_features)`, _algorithms.py:276).
findings.evidence: Line 481: `continuous = [f for f in features if f not in set(cat_features)]`. The expression `set(cat_features)` is part of the `if` clause, so it is constructed afresh on each iteration of `f in features`; the result is identical every time. Compare _auto_terms (line 48-49) which correctly binds `cat_set = set(cat_features)` once before the loop.
findings.est_reduction: 0 net LOC (1 line hoisted into 1 binding + 1 use); removes a per-element set rebuild — micro-perf + consistency with the established cat_set idiom
findings.behavior_preservation: Identical output: f not in set(cat_features) and f not in cat_set are equivalent for every f; only the number of times the set is built changes. No ordering, dtype, or value change.

findings.title: Temporal mask ignores holdout_size when validation_size==0: holdout swallows ALL post-cutoff rows
findings.description: In _temporal_mask the post-cutoff data is split between validation and holdout using holdout_frac = holdout_size / (validation_size + holdout_size). When validation_size == 0 (a valid, explicit request meaning 'no validation set'), this fraction collapses to holdout_size/holdout_size = 1.0, so EVERY post-cutoff row is assigned to holdout regardless of the requested holdout_size. The requested holdout fraction is silently discarded. The subsequent reclassification block (lines 316-318, 'if validation_size == 0: VALIDATION -> TRAIN') cannot help because there are no VALIDATION rows left to convert. This contradicts the documented semantics of holdout_size (a fraction of the dataset, honoured exactly by the sibling _random_mask) and produces a holdout set far larger than requested with no error or warning. The realised holdout fraction equals the entire post-cutoff portion of the data, which is driven by cutoff_date, not by holdout_size at all.
findings.evidence: Executed with venv polars: df of 20 rows, 14 dated 2024-01-01 (pre-cutoff) and 6 dated 2024-08-* (post-cutoff), SplitConfig(strategy='temporal', cutoff_date='2024-06-01', validation_size=0.0, holdout_size=0.1). Result: TRAIN=14, VALIDATION=0, HOLDOUT=6 — i.e. ALL 6 post-cutoff rows (30% of the dataset) became holdout despite holdout_size=0.1 requesting ~2 rows. By direct contrast the SAME config with strategy='random' on 20 rows yields TRAIN=18, VALIDATION=0, HOLDOUT=2, correctly honouring holdout_size=0.1. Code trace: total = validation_size + holdout_size = 0.0 + 0.1 = 0.1; holdout_frac = 0.1/0.1 = 1.0 (line 302); n_holdout = int(len(sorted_non_train) * 1.0) = 6 (line 312); partition[sorted_non_train[-6:]] = HOLDOUT (line 314) marks every post-cutoff row. Reproduced identically with real Date dtype (not just Utf8). validation_size=0 is permitted by __post_init__ (0 <= validation_size) and flows unguarded from user dicts via _train_config.py / _train_service.py SplitConfig(**split).

findings.title: Group mask validation fallback is a no-op when no TRAIN group exists, leaving both validation AND train empty
findings.description: The 'ensure at least one validation group' fallback (lines 352-358) only fires when no group landed in VALIDATION, and it tries to flip the first group that is currently labelled PARTITION_TRAIN into VALIDATION. But when holdout_size is large relative to the (few) groups, it is possible for EVERY unique group to hash below holdout_size and be assigned PARTITION_HOLDOUT — so there is no TRAIN group for the loop to convert. The loop iterates, finds no group with value PARTITION_TRAIN, and breaks out having changed nothing. The result is that validation_size > 0 was requested but the validation partition is silently empty, AND the train partition is also empty (every row is holdout). Training then proceeds on zero rows with no error. The known catalog finding #51 explicitly assumes 'the only correction triggers solely on no_validation' and that it succeeds when it fires; this is the distinct failure mode where the correction fires but is ineffective because its precondition (an available TRAIN group) is not guaranteed.
findings.evidence: Executed with venv polars: df = {'g': ['A','A','B','B','B']} (2 groups), SplitConfig(strategy='group', validation_size=0.2, holdout_size=0.6, seed=2). md5 hash fractions: frac(2,'A')=0.025, frac(2,'B')=0.037, both < holdout_size=0.6, so both groups -> PARTITION_HOLDOUT at lines 344-345. no_validation is True (line 352), validation_size>0 and len(unique_groups)=2>1, so the fallback enters the loop (lines 355-358), but neither A nor B is PARTITION_TRAIN, so nothing is flipped and it breaks. Final mask = [2,2,2,2,2]: TRAIN=0, VALIDATION=0, HOLDOUT=5 — validation requested (0.2) is empty and train is empty. Downstream _training_job._split_data counts n_train/n_validation from this mask and would attempt to train on an empty train partition.

findings.title: _html_table zips body cells against `align` (not the row), silently dropping cells when align is shorter than a row
findings.description: The body-cell loop is `for cell, a in zip(row, align):` (line 50). `zip` stops at the shorter of `row`/`align`, so the number of emitted `<td>` cells is capped at `len(align)`, NOT `len(row)`. If a caller ever passes a row with more cells than the supplied `align` list (or an `align` shorter than the header/row width), the trailing cell value is silently discarded — a column of data vanishes from the rendered table with no error. This is the opposite of the project's stated 'fail loudly' preference: a malformed alignment list produces a silently truncated table rather than an exception. The header loop has the same shape (`zip(headers, align)`, line 44), so a too-short `align` would also drop header columns silently. The correct contract is for cell count to be governed by the row width (e.g. iterate the row and default missing alignments to 'left'), or to assert `len(align) == len(headers)`.
findings.evidence: Line 41 sets `align = ['left'] * len(headers)` ONLY when align is None. Lines 44/50 use `zip(headers, align)` and `zip(row, align)`. With e.g. row=['a','b','c','d'] and align=['left','right','left'], zip yields 3 pairs → only 3 `<td>` emitted; cell 'd' is dropped with no warning. All in-file callers (lines 101,108,116,141-145,172,237) currently pass align/rows consistent with headers, so the path is latent and not exercised by existing tests (tests/test_model_card.py only checks 2-column tables). `_html_table` is private (only used in this file), so the defect is a latent robustness/silent-failure hazard, not an active production bug.

findings.title: Conflicting top-level var_power vs variance_power is silently resolved (var_power wins) instead of failing loud
findings.description: build_training_job_kwargs only raises on a conflict between config['variance_power'] and an EXPLICIT params['var_power'] entry (guarded by params_has_explicit_var_power, which reads the ORIGINAL config['params'] dict). It does not detect the case where a GLM config carries BOTH a top-level 'var_power' alias and a top-level 'variance_power' with different values. In that case the top-level var_power silently overrides the user's variance_power with no error, contradicting the module's explicit 'Keep one Tweedie variance-power source' contract and the project's fail-loudly guideline.
findings.evidence: Take config = {algorithm:'glm', family:'tweedie', var_power: 1.8, variance_power: 1.3} (no 'params' key). (1) build_train_params: algorithm=='glm' loops GLM_CONFIG_KEYS which includes 'var_power'; 'var_power' in config and not in params -> params['var_power']=1.8. The subsequent `config.get('variance_power') is not None and 'var_power' not in params` check at L67 is now False because var_power is in params, so it is skipped. (2) Back in build_training_job_kwargs: raw_params = config.get('params') or {} == {}, so params_has_explicit_var_power = {}.get('var_power') is None -> False. variance_power initial = config.get('variance_power') = 1.3. (3) L114 enters (glm and params.get('var_power')==1.8 not None). L115 condition: config.get('variance_power')=1.3 is not None AND params_has_explicit_var_power(False) -> overall False -> NO raise. L124: variance_power = params['var_power'] = 1.8. Result: the user-supplied variance_power=1.3 is silently discarded in favour of the var_power=1.8 alias, with no conflict error. The existing conflict test (test_glm_conflicting_variance_power_alias_fails_loudly) only covers the variance_power-vs-params['var_power'] path, not variance_power-vs-top-level-var_power.
